title: Applied Anatomy of Injury & Disease
summary: How anatomy predicts the signs, spread and surgical treatment of head and neck injury and disease.

lessons.title: Skull Fractures: The Pterion, Middle Meningeal Artery & Basilar Fracture Signs

levels.kid:
Your skull is like a strong helmet made of many bone pieces joined together. On the side of your head, just above and behind the outer corner of your eye, there is a spot where four bones meet. This spot is called the **pterion** (say "TEER-ee-on"). The bone there is thin, like an eggshell.

Right under that thin spot runs a blood tube called the **middle meningeal artery**. If a hard hit cracks the bone there, the tube can tear. Blood then builds up between the skull and the brain's covering and presses on the brain.

Sometimes a person seems fine at first and then gets very sleepy. That is why doctors take every head bump near the temple seriously.
levels.hs:
The skull isn't one bone. The side of the head is where the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet in an H-shaped junction called the **pterion**. It sits about 3–4 cm above the middle of the zygomatic arch (cheekbone) and is one of the thinnest parts of the skull.

Just inside the pterion runs the anterior branch of the **middle meningeal artery (MMA)**, which supplies the **dura mater**, the tough outer covering of the brain. A blow to the temple can fracture the thin bone and tear the artery. Arterial blood then peels the dura away from the skull, forming an **epidural hematoma**. On a CT scan it looks like a **biconvex (lens-shaped)** collection, and it usually stops at skull **sutures**, where the dura is stuck down tightly.

A classic story is the **lucid interval**: a person is knocked out, wakes up and seems fine, then gets worse over hours as the clot grows.

Fractures can also happen at the **skull base** (basilar fractures). Signs include:
- **Raccoon eyes**: bruising around both eyes
- **Battle's sign**: bruising behind the ear
- Clear fluid (**cerebrospinal fluid**, CSF) leaking from the nose or ear
- Blood behind the eardrum

An example: a teenager hit in the temple by a baseball who later becomes drowsy needs an urgent CT scan.
levels.college:
**Pterion anatomy.** The pterion is the H-shaped sutural junction of the frontal, parietal, squamous temporal and greater wing of the sphenoid. It overlies the anterior (frontal) branch of the **middle meningeal artery**, which often runs in a bony groove or even a short tunnel. It also overlies the lateral sulcus and Broca's area region. The MMA arises from the first (mandibular) part of the **maxillary artery** and enters the middle cranial fossa through the **foramen spinosum**.

**Epidural (extradural) hematoma (EDH).**
- Most often caused by a temporal or temporoparietal fracture tearing the MMA; about 85–90% of EDHs have an associated fracture.
- Blood collects between the inner table and the periosteal dura.
- Because the dura is tightly bound at sutures, EDH rarely crosses them and appears **biconvex**. Subdural hematomas cross sutures, are crescentic and usually come from bridging veins.
- A lucid interval occurs in a minority (often cited as roughly 20–50%).
- Expanding temporal clots push the uncus medially. **Uncal herniation** compresses the oculomotor nerve, giving an ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, and later causes contralateral weakness.

**Basilar skull fractures** usually involve the anterior fossa or the petrous temporal bone.
- **Anterior fossa** (cribriform plate, orbital roof): periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes), CSF rhinorrhea, anosmia.
- **Middle fossa / petrous temporal**: Battle's sign (mastoid ecchymosis, often delayed 1–2 days), hemotympanum, CSF otorrhea, conductive or sensorineural hearing loss, and facial nerve palsy.

CSF leak opens a route for **meningitis**. A ring or halo sign on gauze suggests CSF, but **beta-2 transferrin** is the confirmatory test.
levels.phd:
**Fracture mechanics and the pterion.** Skull thickness varies widely. The squamous temporal bone and the pterion can be only a few millimetres thick, with little diploë, so lateral impacts transmit force to the inner table. The MMA groove is often deep in this region, and in a sizeable minority of skulls the anterior branch passes through a complete bony canal. When this happens, even a hairline fracture can lacerate the vessel. Pterion morphology varies: in the common **sphenoparietal** type the sphenoid and parietal bones meet. Other types are **frontotemporal**, **stellate** and **epipteric** (with a sutural bone), and the type alters the landmarks a surgeon uses.

**Hematoma physiology.** EDH expansion requires arterial pressure to strip the dura off the inner table. The dura is most adherent at sutures and in the young less so in some regions. EDH is relatively uncommon in the elderly, whose dura is more firmly attached, and in infants, whose pliable skulls deform rather than fracture. About 10% of EDHs are venous (from dural sinuses or diploic veins), often in the posterior fossa or at the vertex, and they expand more slowly. Intracranial pressure dynamics follow the **Monro–Kellie doctrine**: CSF and venous blood are displaced until compliance is exhausted, then pressure rises steeply. This explains abrupt deterioration after a lucid interval.

**Herniation signs.** The parasympathetic fibres run superficially on the oculomotor nerve, so uncal compression dilates the pupil before extraocular palsy develops. **Kernohan's notch** phenomenon is a classic false-localizing sign. The contralateral cerebral peduncle is pressed against the tentorial edge, producing weakness on the same side as the lesion.

**Temporal bone fractures.** The traditional longitudinal/transverse scheme has largely given way to **otic capsule–sparing versus otic capsule–violating** classification. Capsule-violating fractures carry substantially higher rates of facial nerve paralysis, sensorineural hearing loss and CSF leak.
levels.expert:
**Imaging and decisions.** Non-contrast CT with bone windows and thin-section reconstruction is standard, and CT angiography is used when a fracture crosses the carotid canal or a dural venous sinus. The **swirl sign** (a mixed-density area within an EDH) indicates active bleeding and predicts expansion. Brain Trauma Foundation guidance supports evacuating an EDH larger than 30 cm³ regardless of GCS. Urgent surgery is also indicated for comatose patients with anisocoria. Smaller EDHs (under about 15 mm thick, midline shift under 5 mm, GCS above 8, no focal deficit) may be observed with serial CT. Temporal and posterior fossa clots warrant a lower threshold because there is less room before brainstem compression.

**Operative anatomy.** Craniotomy centred over the clot is standard; burr holes are a temporizing measure in austere settings. The bleeding MMA is coagulated, and if it bleeds from the foramen spinosum, the foramen can be packed with bone wax. **Dural tack-up sutures** reduce reaccumulation. The pterion is also the key landmark for pterional (frontotemporal) craniotomy.

**Basilar fracture pitfalls.**
- Do not pass nasogastric tubes or nasotracheal airways in suspected anterior fossa fractures, because intracranial placement through the cribriform plate is reported.
- Most traumatic CSF leaks close within about a week with conservative care. Persistent leaks need localization (high-resolution CT, CT or MR cisternography) and endoscopic endonasal or open repair.
- Prophylactic antibiotics for CSF leak are not supported by Cochrane review evidence, while pneumococcal vaccination is commonly recommended.
- Facial palsy of **immediate onset** suggests nerve transection and may need exploration. **Delayed-onset** palsy usually recovers with steroids. Electroneurography helps decide.
- Clival and carotid canal fractures raise concern for blunt cerebrovascular injury and abducens palsy.

**Open questions.** Researchers are working out which small EDHs will expand, and whether early **MMA embolization**, already studied in randomized trials for chronic subdural hematoma, has a role in selected acute cases.

keyPoints: The pterion is the H-shaped junction of frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones
The anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery lies under the thin pterion
MMA tear causes a biconvex epidural hematoma that rarely crosses sutures
Lucid interval, then uncal herniation with an ipsilateral dilated pupil
Basilar fracture signs: raccoon eyes, Battle's sign, hemotympanum, CSF leak
Beta-2 transferrin confirms CSF; avoid nasal tubes in anterior fossa fractures

test.q: Which four bones meet at the pterion?
test.explain: The frontal, parietal, squamous temporal and greater wing of the sphenoid form the H-shaped pterion. The occipital bone lies at the back of the skull.

test.q: The middle meningeal artery enters the skull through the:
test.explain: The MMA comes off the maxillary artery and passes through the foramen spinosum. The foramen ovale carries V3.

test.q: A typical epidural hematoma on CT looks:
test.explain: The dura is bound tightly at sutures, so an EDH is biconvex and stops at them. Crescentic clots that cross sutures are subdural.

test.q: Subdural hematomas most often come from:
test.explain: Bridging veins cross the subdural space and tear with shearing. MMA tears cause epidural clots.

test.q: An expanding temporal EDH causes uncal herniation. The earliest eye sign is usually:
choices: A small pupil on the opposite side
A dilated pupil on the same side
Loss of vision in both eyes
test.explain: The uncus compresses the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve, whose superficial parasympathetic fibres are affected first, producing a dilated pupil.

test.q: Bruising behind the ear over the mastoid is called:
test.explain: Battle's sign suggests a petrous temporal (middle fossa) fracture and often appears after a delay of a day or two.

test.q: Raccoon eyes with clear fluid dripping from the nose suggest a fracture of the:
test.explain: Cribriform plate and orbital roof fractures cause periorbital bruising and CSF rhinorrhea.

test.q: Which nerve is classically injured in a petrous temporal bone fracture?
test.explain: The facial nerve runs through the temporal bone, so these fractures can cause facial palsy along with hearing loss.

test.q: What is the main infectious danger of a CSF leak?
test.explain: A leak connects the subarachnoid space to the nose or ear, letting bacteria reach the meninges.

test.q: A patient wakes after a blow, seems fine, then worsens. This is the lucid ___.
test.explain: The lucid interval reflects a period of compensation before the growing clot raises pressure.

test.q: Which protein test confirms that nasal fluid is CSF?
test.explain: Beta-2 transferrin is found in CSF and not in nasal mucus, so it is the confirmatory test.

test.q: Blood behind the eardrum after a skull base fracture is called ___.
test.explain: Hemotympanum is a sign of a petrous temporal fracture.

kidTest.q: Where is the pterion?
choices: On the side of the head
At the back of the neck
kidTest.explain: It sits on the side of the head, above and behind the outer corner of the eye.

kidTest.q: What is the bone like at the pterion?
kidTest.explain: The bone there is thin, so it can crack more easily.

kidTest.q: What runs just under that thin spot?
kidTest.explain: The middle meningeal artery is a blood tube that runs under the pterion.

kidTest.q: If the tube tears, what happens?
kidTest.explain: Blood builds up between the skull and the brain's covering and presses on the brain.

kidTest.q: Your skull is like a strong h _ _ _ _ _ for your brain.
kidTest.explain: The skull protects the brain the way a helmet does.

advancedTest.q: Why are epidural hematomas relatively uncommon in elderly patients?
choices: Their bridging veins absorb the impact forces
Their dura is more firmly attached to the skull
Their skulls are too pliable to fracture
Their middle meningeal artery is usually absent
advancedTest.explain: Arterial pressure has to strip the dura off the bone, and this is harder when the dura is firmly adherent. Pliable skulls belong to infants, not the elderly.

advancedTest.q: A right temporal EDH produces right-sided limb weakness. The best explanation is:
choices: Direct pressure on the right motor cortex
A second clot in the left hemisphere
Compression of the right oculomotor nucleus
The left peduncle compressed against the tentorium
advancedTest.explain: In Kernohan's notch phenomenon, the contralateral peduncle is pushed against the tentorial edge. This gives weakness on the same side as the lesion, a false-localizing sign.

advancedTest.q: Why does deterioration after a lucid interval tend to be abrupt?
choices: Compliance is exhausted, so pressure climbs steeply
The fracture line widens and lets the clot drain out
The dura reattaches to the skull at the sutures
Venous bleeding suddenly turns into arterial bleeding
advancedTest.explain: Under the Monro–Kellie doctrine, CSF and venous blood are displaced first. Once that reserve is used up, small volume increases cause large pressure rises.

advancedTest.q: Facial palsy that is complete at the moment of a temporal bone fracture, rather than delayed, most suggests:
choices: Possible transection that may need exploration
Swelling of an intact nerve that will recover
A CSF leak that will close within a week
Damage to the hypoglossal nerve instead
advancedTest.explain: Immediate-onset palsy suggests the nerve is disrupted, so exploration may be needed. Delayed-onset palsy usually reflects edema and tends to recover.

lessons.title: Facial Fractures: Le Fort Patterns, Orbital Blowout & Mandible

levels.kid:
Your face has a strong frame of bones, a bit like the beams in a house. Some beams are thick and strong. Others are thin like eggshells.

When the face gets a hard hit, the bones crack along their weak lines. Doctors noticed the cracks often follow the same paths, and they gave those paths names.

The bone under your eye is very thin. A hit from a ball can push it down into the space below, like a trapdoor. Then the eye can't move up properly, and the person sees double.

Your jaw bone is shaped like a horseshoe. A horseshoe often breaks in two places at once, so doctors always look for a second crack. Fixing the bones helps teeth fit together again.
levels.hs:
The face is built from thick **buttresses** (pillars of bone that carry chewing forces) joined by thin plates. Fractures tend to follow the thin areas.

**Le Fort fractures**: In 1901 René Le Fort dropped weights on cadaver heads and found three classic fracture lines. All three break through the **pterygoid plates** at the back, separating the upper jaw (maxilla) from the skull:
- **Le Fort I**: horizontal, just above the teeth. The tooth-bearing part of the upper jaw moves on its own.
- **Le Fort II**: pyramid-shaped, through the nose bridge and the floor of the eye socket.
- **Le Fort III**: **craniofacial disjunction**. The whole face separates from the skull.

**Orbital blowout fracture**: A blunt object larger than the eye socket, like a fist or a ball, raises pressure inside the orbit. The thin **floor** (or the paper-thin medial wall) breaks outward. Fat and the **inferior rectus** muscle can get trapped, causing **double vision** when looking up. Numbness of the cheek happens because the **infraorbital nerve** runs in the floor.

**Mandible fractures**: The lower jaw is a ring, so it often breaks in two places. A common pair is the **condyle** on one side and the body or angle on the other. Teeth that no longer meet properly (**malocclusion**) is a key sign.
levels.college:
**Buttress anatomy** explains facial fracture patterns. Vertical buttresses (nasomaxillary, zygomaticomaxillary, pterygomaxillary) carry occlusal load. Horizontal buttresses (frontal bar, infraorbital rims, palate, mandible) resist sideways forces. Fixation with plates restores buttress continuity.

**Le Fort patterns** (all involve the pterygoid plates):
- **I (transverse)**: nasal aperture floor, lower maxillary sinus walls, pterygoid plates. The palate and alveolus move as one free piece.
- **II (pyramidal)**: nasofrontal junction, frontal process of the maxilla, medial orbit, orbital floor, inferior orbital rim near the zygomaticomaxillary suture, pterygoid plates. Infraorbital nerve numbness is common.
- **III (craniofacial disjunction)**: nasofrontal junction, across the orbits through the zygomaticofrontal suture and zygomatic arch, then the pterygoid plates. The face hangs loose. CSF rhinorrhea is possible.
On exam, rock the upper incisors and palate. A mobile palate alone suggests I, the nasal bridge moving with it suggests II, and the whole midface moving suggests III. Real injuries are often mixed or differ from side to side.

**Orbital blowout**: Two mechanisms are proposed: a hydraulic rise in orbital pressure, and buckling transmitted from a blow to the rim. The floor fails medial to the **infraorbital groove**. The lamina papyracea of the ethmoid can also fail.
- Upgaze diplopia comes from entrapment of the inferior rectus or its fascial attachments.
- **Enophthalmos** (sunken eye) results from an enlarged orbital volume.
- Infraorbital nerve hypoesthesia affects the cheek, upper lip and upper teeth.

**Mandible**: Common sites are the condyle, angle, body and symphysis/parasymphysis. Muscle pull decides whether fragments shift. At the angle, masseter and medial pterygoid pull upward; the lateral pterygoid pulls a condyle fragment forward and inward. A fracture whose line resists these pulls is called **favorable**. Signs include malocclusion, step deformity and numb lower lip. Lower lip numbness means the **inferior alveolar nerve** has been injured in the mandibular canal.
levels.phd:
Le Fort's 1901 experiments defined lines of weakness, but CT-era work shows how idealized they are. Pure, symmetric Le Fort fractures are uncommon. Wide plate fixation and modern injury mechanisms changed the picture, so descriptive systems now record each buttress separately. A widely cited refinement (Hopper and colleagues, RadioGraphics 2006) offered key CT features for quick classification:
- **Pterygoid plate fracture**: required for any Le Fort.
- **Anterolateral margin of the nasal fossa**: unique to Le Fort I.
- **Inferior orbital rim**: unique to Le Fort II.
- **Zygomatic arch**: unique to Le Fort III.
A caveat: pterygoid plate fractures also occur without a Le Fort pattern, as in zygomaticomaxillary complex (ZMC) fractures.

**ZMC ("tripod" or tetrapod) fractures** separate the zygoma at four points: the zygomaticofrontal suture, the zygomatic arch, the zygomaticomaxillary buttress/infraorbital rim, and the zygomaticosphenoid articulation of the lateral orbital wall. The zygomaticosphenoid suture is the best indicator of how well the bone has been realigned. Malar flattening and trismus can occur when the arch impinges on the coronoid process.

**Blowout biomechanics**: Smith and Regan's hydraulic theory (1957) is the classic explanation. Fujino's cadaver work supported buckling from rim impact. Waterhouse's studies suggested both mechanisms act, producing different fracture sizes. The posteromedial floor is thinnest. In the inferior orbital fissure region the floor slopes upward, which matters when reconstructing orbital volume.

**Pediatric "white-eyed" blowout**: Elastic bone in children cracks and springs back like a trapdoor, strangling the inferior rectus. There is little bruising. Ischemia can cause the **oculocardiac reflex**: trigeminal afferent input drives a vagal response, leading to bradycardia, nausea and syncope. This is an indication for urgent release.

**Mandibular mechanics**: Treating the mandible as a ring predicts paired fractures. Champy's lines of ideal osteosynthesis place monocortical miniplates along tension zones. This allows load-sharing rather than load-bearing fixation and lets the patient chew earlier. Load-bearing reconstruction plates are still used for comminuted or atrophic edentulous fractures. Condylar management is a long-running controversy: closed treatment versus open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF), weighing facial nerve risk against restored ramus height and occlusion.
levels.expert:
Several practical points change management in facial trauma.

**Airway and bleeding first.** A Le Fort fracture that is displaced backward along the skull base can obstruct the airway. Bilateral parasymphyseal mandible fractures can remove the tongue's support through genioglossus attachments, letting the tongue fall back. Severe midface bleeding from internal maxillary artery branches may need nasal packing, reduction or angioembolization.

**Skull-base caution.** Suspected Le Fort II/III or nasoorbitoethmoid injury raises concern for cribriform disruption. Blind nasogastric or nasotracheal tubes are avoided. Submental intubation is an option when the patient must bite together during surgery but a tracheostomy is not wanted.

**Eye red flags.** Every orbital fracture needs visual acuity and pupil testing. A relative afferent pupillary defect, retrobulbar hematoma or orbital compartment syndrome (proptosis, a tense globe, falling vision) needs emergent lateral canthotomy and cantholysis before fracture repair. The orbital apex lies close to the optic canal, so traumatic optic neuropathy must be considered. Corticosteroids are no longer routinely supported after the CRASH and IONTS data.

**Indications for orbital floor repair.** These include entrapment with a non-resolving oculocardiac reflex (immediate); early enophthalmos or hypoglobus; and large defects (often cited as about 50% of the floor, or more than roughly 1 to 2 cm²) that predict late enophthalmos. Forced duction testing tells true entrapment apart from swelling or nerve palsy. Implants include titanium mesh and patient-specific implants. Intraoperative navigation and mirror-image virtual planning from the uninjured side now refine orbital volume restoration.

**NOE fractures.** The Markowitz-Manson classification depends on the medial canthal tendon fragment. Telecanthus signals avulsion and needs transnasal canthopexy.

**Mandible pitfalls.** Teeth in the fracture line are a site of infection. Antibiotics beyond the perioperative period have not clearly helped. Lower lip numbness lasting longer than expected deserves documentation for medicolegal reasons. Restoring occlusion with maxillomandibular fixation before plating is the rule. Panfacial fractures are sequenced "bottom-up/outside-in" or the reverse, a debated choice. Open questions include virtual surgical planning cost-benefit, resorbable fixation in growing children, and the best timing for condylar ORIF.

keyPoints: Facial bones break along thin areas between strong vertical and horizontal buttresses
All Le Fort fractures involve the pterygoid plates
Le Fort I is transverse, II is pyramidal, III is craniofacial disjunction
Blowout fractures break the thin orbital floor; inferior rectus entrapment causes upgaze diplopia
Infraorbital nerve numbness signals orbital floor or midface injury
The mandible is a ring, so it often fractures in two places; malocclusion is a key sign

test.q: Which structure is fractured in every Le Fort pattern?
test.explain: Pterygoid plate fracture is required for all Le Fort types. The zygomatic arch is specific to Le Fort III, and the inferior orbital rim to Le Fort II.

test.q: A Le Fort III fracture is best described as:
choices: A break of the lower jaw ring
A horizontal break just above the teeth
A pyramid through the nasal bridge
Separation of the face from the skull
test.explain: Le Fort III is craniofacial disjunction: the whole midface separates from the cranial base.

test.q: After a ball hits his eye, a player sees double only when looking up. The likely trapped muscle is the:
test.explain: In an orbital floor blowout, the inferior rectus can be entrapped in the fracture, limiting upgaze.

test.q: Cheek and upper lip numbness after an orbital floor fracture points to injury of the:
test.explain: The infraorbital nerve runs in the orbital floor and supplies the cheek, upper lip and upper teeth. The inferior alveolar nerve supplies the lower lip.

test.q: Why does the mandible often break in two places?
choices: Its muscles snap it in half
It behaves like a bony ring
Its teeth weaken the whole bone
test.explain: As a horseshoe-shaped ring hinged at both joints, a force often causes a second fracture, such as a contralateral condyle.

test.q: In a Le Fort I fracture, the freely mobile segment contains the:
test.explain: Le Fort I runs horizontally above the teeth, freeing the palate and alveolus as one piece.

test.q: A sunken eye after a large blowout fracture is called:
test.explain: Enophthalmos results when the orbit's volume enlarges. Proptosis is a forward-pushed eye.

test.q: Lower lip numbness after a mandible body fracture suggests damage to the:
test.explain: The inferior alveolar nerve runs in the mandibular canal and ends as the mental nerve to the lower lip.

test.q: Which fracture line is described as pyramidal?
test.explain: Le Fort II passes through the nasal bridge, medial orbit, orbital floor and pterygoid plates in a pyramid shape.

test.q: Teeth that no longer meet properly after a jaw fracture are described by what term?
test.explain: Malocclusion is a key sign of mandible or maxillary fractures.

test.q: The thick pillars of facial bone that carry chewing forces are called ___.
test.explain: Fractures tend to occur in thin bone between the buttresses, and fixation restores them.

test.q: Which French surgeon described three classic midface fracture lines in 1901?
test.explain: René Le Fort mapped the fracture lines using cadaver experiments.

kidTest.q: Which bone near the eye is thin like an eggshell?
kidTest.explain: The floor under the eye is very thin and can crack like a trapdoor.

kidTest.q: If the bone under the eye breaks, what can happen?
kidTest.explain: A trapped eye muscle can't move well, so the person sees double.

kidTest.q: What shape is the jaw bone?
kidTest.explain: The jaw is shaped like a horseshoe, so it often breaks in two places.

kidTest.q: Why do doctors look for a second jaw crack?
choices: The jaw often breaks in two spots
The jaw has two hearts inside
The jaw grows back very fast
kidTest.explain: Because the jaw is a ring shape, one hit often causes two cracks.

kidTest.q: When a face bone breaks, doctors call it a f _ _ _ _ _ _ _. What is the word?
kidTest.explain: A fracture is a broken or cracked bone.

advancedTest.q: A CT shows pterygoid plate and zygomatic arch fractures but an intact inferior orbital rim and nasal fossa margin. The best fit is:
advancedTest.explain: Zygomatic arch involvement is unique to Le Fort III among Le Fort types. The intact rim argues against II, and the intact nasal fossa margin argues against I.

advancedTest.q: A child with an orbital floor fracture has little bruising, restricted upgaze, bradycardia and vomiting. Why is surgery urgent?
choices: Infraorbital nerve injury is causing a vagal storm
Cerebrospinal fluid is leaking through the cribriform plate
A trapdoor fracture is strangling the inferior rectus
Retrobulbar bleeding is compressing the optic nerve
advancedTest.explain: Elastic pediatric bone snaps back and traps the muscle. Its ischemia drives the oculocardiac reflex, an indication for urgent release.

advancedTest.q: Champy's principle allows small monocortical plates because they:
choices: Carry the full chewing load without help from bone
Neutralize tension along lines where bone fragments separate
Replace the need for occlusion during the repair
Avoid the mandibular canal by sitting at the lower border
advancedTest.explain: Miniplates on tension lines provide load-sharing fixation; compression forces are carried by the bone itself.

advancedTest.q: A Le Fort II patient needs urgent airway management. Which choice is most anatomically concerning?
choices: Oral intubation with a cuffed tube
advancedTest.explain: Midface fractures may disrupt the cribriform plate, so blind nasal tubes risk intracranial passage.

lessons.title: Deep Neck Infections, the Danger Space & Septic Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis

levels.kid:
Your neck is packed with tubes and wires: a tube for food, a tube for air, big blood vessels, and nerves. Thin, slippery wrappings called **fascia** wrap them, like plastic wrap around sandwiches.

Between the wrappings are flat gaps, like hallways. Most of the time they are empty. But if germs from a bad tooth or sore throat get in, pus can slide down a hallway like water down a slide. One hallway is so long it reaches all the way into the chest. Doctors call it the **danger space**.

Germs on the face can travel too. Veins near your nose can carry them backward to a pool of blood behind your eyes. That is why doctors take a swollen, red face with eye problems very seriously.
levels.hs:
The neck is divided by sheets of connective tissue called **deep cervical fascia**. The potential spaces between these sheets are normally collapsed, but infection can fill them with pus and spread along them. This is a **deep neck infection**.

Common sources:
- **Teeth**, especially infected lower molars, which is the most common source in adults.
- **Tonsils and throat**, which is common in children.

Key spaces:
- **Peritonsillar abscess** ("quinsy"): pus beside a tonsil. The patient has a muffled "hot potato" voice, trouble opening the mouth (**trismus**), and the uvula pushed to the opposite side.
- **Ludwig's angina**: a fast-spreading infection of the floor of the mouth on both sides. It pushes the tongue up and back and can block the airway.
- **Retropharyngeal space**: behind the throat.
- **Danger space**: just behind the retropharyngeal space. It runs from the skull base down into the chest. Pus here can cause **mediastinitis**, a life-threatening infection around the heart.

The face has a related hazard. Veins of the central face around the nose and upper lip connect to the **cavernous sinus**, a venous channel beside the pituitary gland. Their valves are absent or work poorly. Infection can travel backward and cause **septic cavernous sinus thrombosis**, a dangerous infected clot. Signs include a bulging eye, a swollen eyelid and trouble moving the eye.
levels.college:
**Fascial anatomy.** The deep cervical fascia has three layers:
- **Superficial (investing) layer**: surrounds the neck and splits around the sternocleidomastoid, the trapezius, and the submandibular and parotid glands.
- **Middle layer** (pretracheal/visceral, including **buccopharyngeal fascia**): wraps the pharynx, esophagus, larynx, trachea and thyroid.
- **Deep (prevertebral) layer**: covers the vertebrae and surrounding muscles. It splits into an anterior **alar** layer and the true prevertebral layer.

**Three spaces behind the pharynx**, from front to back:
- **Retropharyngeal space**: lies between the buccopharyngeal fascia and the alar fascia. It ends at about T1-T2, where these layers fuse. In children it contains lymph nodes that drain the nasopharynx, adenoids and sinuses. These nodes shrink in later childhood, which is why retropharyngeal abscess is mostly a disease of young children.
- **Danger space**: lies between the alar and prevertebral layers. It runs from the skull base to the diaphragm, giving a direct path to the posterior mediastinum.
- **Prevertebral space**: lies behind the prevertebral fascia and extends to the coccyx. It is classically involved in vertebral osteomyelitis or tuberculosis (Pott's disease).

**Parapharyngeal space**: an inverted pyramid from the skull base to the hyoid. The styloid process and its muscles divide it into two compartments:
- **Prestyloid**: contains fat and deep parotid tissue. Infection causes trismus because it irritates the medial pterygoid.
- **Poststyloid**: contains the carotid sheath and cranial nerves IX-XII.

**Ludwig's angina**: a bilateral cellulitis of the sublingual and submandibular spaces. The mylohyoid line explains which teeth seed which space. Molar roots, especially the second and third molars, lie below the line, so they drain to the submandibular space.

**Cavernous sinus pathway.** The facial vein connects to the cavernous sinus through the angular vein, the **superior ophthalmic vein** and the pterygoid plexus. Because these veins have few or ineffective valves, infection from the "danger triangle" of the face, or from the sphenoid or ethmoid sinuses, can reach the sinus. The sinus contains CN III, IV, V1, V2 and VI and the internal carotid artery. Most signs therefore come from these structures:
- **Abducens (VI) palsy**: often first, because the nerve floats free in the sinus.
- **Proptosis and chemosis**: from blocked venous drainage of the orbit.
levels.phd:
**Microbiology.** Odontogenic deep neck infections are polymicrobial. They usually involve viridans streptococci, especially the *S. anginosus* (milleri) group, mixed with anaerobes such as *Prevotella*, *Fusobacterium* and *Peptostreptococcus*. Septic cavernous sinus thrombosis (CST) is caused mainly by *Staphylococcus aureus*, increasingly methicillin-resistant (MRSA). Sphenoid sinusitis has now overtaken facial furuncles as the leading source. In diabetic ketoacidosis or neutropenia, **mucormycosis** can invade the cavernous sinus and internal carotid artery directly.

**Lemierre syndrome.** This is septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein, classically caused by *Fusobacterium necrophorum*. It follows pharyngitis or parapharyngeal infection and is followed by septic emboli to the lungs. It shows how poststyloid involvement turns a local abscess into a blood-borne disease. The carotid sheath can also be eroded, producing a carotid pseudoaneurysm or a "herald bleed".

**Why the danger space is dangerous.** The alar fascia is thin. Retropharyngeal pus can break through it into the danger space, which has no lower barrier above the diaphragm. **Descending necrotizing mediastinitis** has historically had mortality around 30-40%. Spread by gravity, negative intrathoracic pressure and loose connective tissue drives the descent. The Endo classification grades mediastinal involvement:
- Type I: above the carina.
- Type IIA: lower anterior mediastinum.
- Type IIB: lower anterior and posterior mediastinum.

Type II disease usually needs thoracic drainage, not cervical drainage alone.

**Pathophysiology of CST.** The intercavernous sinuses connect the two cavernous sinuses, so CST often begins on one side and becomes bilateral within 24-48 hours. A contralateral eye sign strongly suggests CST over orbital cellulitis. Inflammation narrows the cavernous ICA, which can cause stroke. Pituitary involvement can cause hypopituitarism. Mortality was close to universal before antibiotics. It is now often quoted at about 10-30%, with lasting cranial nerve deficits common in survivors.

**Debates.** The anatomy of valveless facial veins has been challenged. Cadaver work suggests valves exist in the facial and ophthalmic veins but do not reliably direct flow, and flow can reverse with venous pressure changes. Anticoagulation in septic CST is still debated, since no randomized trials exist. Retrospective series suggest lower morbidity when it is started early, but intracranial hemorrhage risk is real.
levels.expert:
**Imaging and diagnostic pitfalls.**
- Contrast-enhanced CT is the workhorse for deep neck infection. However, a rim-enhancing hypodensity predicts actual pus with only about 75-80% accuracy, so phlegmon versus abscess can be wrong in both directions.
- On a lateral neck X-ray, prevertebral soft tissue wider than about 7 mm at C2 in adults is suspicious. Neck flexion and crying in infants create false widening.
- For CST, MRI with venography shows filling defects, an enlarged convex lateral sinus wall and a dilated superior ophthalmic vein. CT venography is a reasonable alternative.
- Always image the chest when neck disease reaches below the hyoid or the patient worsens despite drainage, because mediastinal extension is often missed clinically.

**Airway first.** In Ludwig's angina and large retropharyngeal collections, the decisive event is airway loss, not sepsis.
- Avoid sedation and paralysis before the airway is secured. Losing muscle tone can turn a narrowed airway into a "cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate" emergency.
- Preferred approaches are awake fiberoptic intubation or awake tracheostomy under local anaesthetic. Video laryngoscopy has broadened options, but equipment for an emergency surgical airway should be ready.

**Management trends.**
- Small (under about 2-2.5 cm), well-defined pediatric retropharyngeal and parapharyngeal abscesses often resolve with intravenous antibiotics alone, so the threshold for drainage has risen.
- Image-guided needle aspiration is an alternative to open drainage in selected cases.
- Descending mediastinitis requires cervical drainage plus transthoracic or video-assisted thoracoscopic (VATS) drainage. Combined approaches lowered mortality in modern series.

**Neurosurgical relevance.**
- A prevertebral or epidural extension can compress the cord. Neck pain with new limb weakness requires spinal MRI.
- Sphenoid sinusitis causing CST may need endoscopic sinus drainage.
- In CST, consider corticosteroids only for suspected adrenal insufficiency, since evidence for routine use is weak.
- Watch for mycotic ICA aneurysm in the cavernous segment, which can rupture into the sinus and create a carotid-cavernous fistula.

**Open questions.** Open questions include anticoagulation in septic CST, the role of steroids in reducing airway oedema, and how the rising share of resistant organisms should shape empirical antibiotic choice.

keyPoints: Deep cervical fascia has investing, middle (visceral) and deep (prevertebral, with alar) layers
Danger space lies between alar and prevertebral fascia, from skull base to diaphragm
Retropharyngeal space ends near T1-T2; prevertebral space extends to the coccyx
Lower molar roots below the mylohyoid line seed the submandibular space (Ludwig's angina)
Facial and ophthalmic veins with poorly working valves link the face to the cavernous sinus
Abducens palsy, proptosis and spread to the other eye suggest septic cavernous sinus thrombosis

test.q: The danger space lies between which two fascial layers?
test.explain: The danger space lies between the alar and prevertebral layers. The retropharyngeal space lies in front of it, between the buccopharyngeal and alar fascia.

test.q: Why is the danger space so named?
choices: It extends down to the diaphragm
It lies inside the carotid sheath
test.explain: It runs from the skull base to the diaphragm, giving pus a path into the posterior mediastinum.

test.q: Ludwig's angina is an infection of which region?
choices: Floor of the mouth on both sides
test.explain: It is a bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces that can push the tongue back and block the airway.

test.q: Infected lower second and third molars usually spread to the submandibular space because their roots lie:
test.explain: Roots below the mylohyoid line drain into the submandibular space, beneath the mylohyoid muscle.

test.q: Which sign is typical of a peritonsillar abscess?
choices: Loss of taste on the tongue tip
Uvula pushed to the opposite side
test.explain: Quinsy pushes the uvula away from the affected side and causes a muffled voice and trismus.

test.q: Why is retropharyngeal abscess most common in young children?
choices: Their teeth are more often infected
Their fascia is absent at birth
test.explain: Retropharyngeal lymph nodes drain the nasopharynx and sinuses in young children, then shrink in later childhood.

test.q: Which cranial nerve palsy is often the earliest sign of cavernous sinus thrombosis?
test.explain: CN VI runs free in the sinus beside the internal carotid artery, while III and IV are protected in the lateral wall. CN VII does not pass through the sinus.

test.q: Which vein links the orbit and face directly to the cavernous sinus?
test.explain: The superior ophthalmic vein joins the angular and facial veins to the cavernous sinus.

test.q: Infection of the poststyloid parapharyngeal space threatens which structures?
choices: Carotid sheath and cranial nerves IX-XII
test.explain: The poststyloid compartment holds the carotid sheath and the lower cranial nerves. The prestyloid compartment contains fat and parotid tissue.

test.q: Painful difficulty opening the mouth, caused by muscle spasm, is called ___.
test.explain: Trismus occurs when infection irritates the muscles of chewing, such as the medial pterygoid.

test.q: What is the term for infection of the tissue around the heart in the middle of the chest, a feared result of danger space spread?
test.explain: Pus can descend through the danger space into the mediastinum.

test.q: The retropharyngeal space ends at about vertebral level T1-T2, while the prevertebral space extends down to the ___.
test.explain: The prevertebral space runs the whole length of the spine.

kidTest.q: What are the thin wrappings around parts of the neck called?
kidTest.explain: Fascia wraps neck parts like plastic wrap.

kidTest.q: Where can germs come from to start a deep neck infection?
kidTest.explain: Bad teeth and sore throats are common starting points.

kidTest.q: How far can the danger space hallway reach?
kidTest.explain: The danger space runs from the skull down into the chest.

kidTest.q: Germs on the face near the nose can travel through veins to:
choices: A blood pool behind the eyes
kidTest.explain: Face veins connect to the cavernous sinus behind the eyes.

kidTest.q: Germs in the neck can make thick yellow stuff called p _ _.
kidTest.explain: Pus is made of germs and dead white blood cells.

advancedTest.q: A patient with presumed orbital cellulitis of the left eye develops proptosis and a lateral gaze palsy in the right eye. What is the best anatomical explanation?
choices: Optic chiasm compression by pus from the sphenoid sinus
Spread of infection along the right pterygopalatine fossa
Spread through the intercavernous sinuses to the other cavernous sinus
Retrograde flow through the external jugular vein of the right side
advancedTest.explain: The intercavernous sinuses connect the two cavernous sinuses. Signs in the other eye point to cavernous sinus thrombosis rather than orbital cellulitis alone.

advancedTest.q: A child with a retropharyngeal abscess is drained, but later develops chest pain and a widened mediastinum. Which fascial event best explains this?
choices: Pus followed the parotid duct toward the chest
Pus broke through the alar fascia into the danger space
Pus collected inside the investing layer of fascia
Pus tracked along the carotid sheath to the arm
advancedTest.explain: The retropharyngeal space ends at about T1-T2. Breaking through the thin alar fascia allows descent through the danger space toward the diaphragm.

advancedTest.q: A teenager with recent pharyngitis has a swollen, tender neck along one side and develops lung lesions from septic emboli. Which structure is most likely infected?
choices: Retropharyngeal lymph nodes behind the pharynx
Prestyloid parapharyngeal fat near the parotid
Internal jugular vein in the poststyloid space
advancedTest.explain: This is Lemierre syndrome: septic internal jugular thrombophlebitis that sends emboli to the lungs. The other spaces do not drain directly into a major vein that leads to the lungs.

advancedTest.q: Before intubating a patient with Ludwig's angina, giving sedation and muscle relaxation is discouraged mainly because:
choices: Losing muscle tone can collapse an already narrowed airway
Sedatives increase venous flow into the cavernous sinus
Relaxation causes the abducens nerve to become paralyzed
The drugs spread infection into the danger space
advancedTest.explain: Muscle tone is what keeps the narrowed airway open. Losing it can turn a narrowed airway into one that cannot be intubated or oxygenated, so awake techniques are preferred.

lessons.title: Carotid and Vertebral Dissection and Carotid Endarterectomy Anatomy

levels.kid:
Your neck has four big pipes that carry blood up to your brain. Two are in the front, called the **carotid arteries**. Two are in the back, tucked inside the bones of your neck, called the **vertebral arteries**.

Each pipe has layers, like a garden hose with a lining inside. Sometimes the lining gets a small tear. Blood sneaks in between the layers. That is called a **dissection**. The pipe can get narrow, or a little clot can form and float up to the brain. That can cause a stroke.

Sometimes a carotid pipe gets clogged with sticky gunk called plaque. Surgeons can open the pipe and clean it out. They must be careful, because tiny nerves lie right next to it.
levels.hs:
Four arteries supply the brain. The two **internal carotid arteries (ICAs)** run up the front of the neck, and the two **vertebral arteries** climb through holes in the neck vertebrae before joining inside the skull.

An artery wall has three layers: the inner **intima**, the muscular **media**, and the outer **adventitia**. In a **dissection**, a tear in the intima lets blood push into the wall, forming an **intramural hematoma**. This can narrow the artery or create a rough surface where clots form and travel to the brain (**embolism**). Dissection is one of the leading causes of stroke in people under about 50. It can follow neck trauma, sometimes minor, such as a sports injury.

Clues include:
- Neck, face or head pain on one side
- For carotid dissection: a droopy eyelid and small pupil (**Horner syndrome**)
- For vertebral dissection: pain at the back of the neck plus dizziness or balance problems

Older adults more often develop **atherosclerosis**, plaque that builds up where the common carotid splits into internal and external branches (the **carotid bifurcation**). If a narrowed carotid causes symptoms, surgeons may perform a **carotid endarterectomy (CEA)**: they open the artery and peel out the plaque. Nearby nerves, especially the **hypoglossal nerve** that moves the tongue, must be protected.
levels.college:
**Vessel course.** The common carotid ascends in the carotid sheath with the internal jugular vein (lateral) and vagus nerve (posterior). It divides near the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (about C3-C4). The cervical ICA has no branches. It enters the carotid canal and is relatively fixed at the skull base, so its distal cervical segment is the usual site of spontaneous dissection. The vertebral artery has four segments: V1 (origin to the C6 transverse foramen), V2 (through the transverse foramina of C6-C1), V3 (looping over the posterior arch of the atlas), and V4 (through the dura to join the basilar). V3, the mobile segment at C1-C2, is where vertebral dissections cluster.

**Why dissection causes its signs.**
- An expanding ICA wall stretches the **sympathetic plexus** on its surface. This gives a partial Horner syndrome: ptosis and miosis, usually without loss of facial sweating, because the sudomotor fibers to the face travel with the external carotid.
- Lower cranial nerve palsies (especially CN XII) can arise from compression near the skull base.
- Vertebral dissection gives occipital pain and posterior circulation ischemia. A classic result is lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome from PICA territory infarction.

**CEA anatomy.** The incision follows the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid. Key steps and structures:
- Retract SCM laterally and the jugular vein laterally. Ligate the **common facial vein**, which marks the bifurcation.
- The **hypoglossal nerve** crosses superficial to the ICA and ECA, often a few centimetres above the bifurcation. The **ansa cervicalis** descends from it and may be divided.
- The **vagus** lies posterior in the sheath. Its recurrent laryngeal branch can be injured by retraction, causing hoarseness.
- The **marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve** is at risk with high exposure.
- The **carotid sinus** at the bifurcation, innervated by the glossopharyngeal (Hering) nerve, can trigger bradycardia and hypotension when manipulated.
levels.phd:
**Dissection pathology.** Dissection is fundamentally an intramural hematoma, entering the media either through an intimal tear or from rupture of vasa vasorum. Subintimal tracking causes stenosis or occlusion. Subadventitial tracking produces a **dissecting pseudoaneurysm**. Most strokes are thought to be thromboembolic rather than hemodynamic: imaging often shows distal emboli and territorial infarcts despite good collateral flow.

**Predisposition.** Cervical artery dissection is mainly spontaneous or follows minor trauma, against a background of connective tissue susceptibility. Associations include:
- **Fibromuscular dysplasia**
- Monogenic disorders such as vascular Ehlers-Danlos (COL3A1), Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome
- Recent infection, migraine and cervical manipulation

Genome-wide studies (CADISP consortium) found a risk locus at **PHACTR1**, which is shared with migraine and fibromuscular dysplasia. Skin biopsies show subclinical ultrastructural collagen abnormalities in many patients. This supports a generalized arteriopathy rather than a purely mechanical injury.

**Imaging hallmarks.** On fat-saturated T1 MRI, a crescentic intramural hematoma appears bright once methemoglobin forms. Angiography shows a tapered "flame" occlusion, the "string sign", or a double lumen with an intimal flap.

**Atherosclerotic disease and CEA evidence.** Flow separation at the outer wall of the carotid bulb creates a zone of low, oscillatory wall shear stress. Endothelial gene expression there becomes pro-atherogenic, which explains why plaque localizes to the bifurcation. **NASCET** (1991) measured stenosis as residual lumen against the normal distal ICA. It showed large benefit from CEA in symptomatic stenosis of 70-99% and modest benefit at 50-69%. ECST used a bulb-diameter denominator, so its percentages are not interchangeable with NASCET's. Benefit is time-dependent and is greatest when surgery is done within about two weeks of the event. The asymptomatic trials ACAS and ACST showed small absolute benefits.

**Nuance.** Whether antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy is better for dissection was tested in CADISS (no clear difference) and TREAT-CAD. TREAT-CAD failed to show that aspirin was noninferior to vitamin K antagonists, which leaves the question genuinely open.
levels.expert:
**Clinical pitfalls in dissection.**
- Isolated painful Horner syndrome is ICA dissection until proven otherwise. It warrants urgent vessel imaging (CTA or MRA with fat-sat T1).
- Early MRI can miss the intramural hematoma before methemoglobin forms.
- Vertebral V3 and V4 dissections can extend intracranially. Intracranial dissections lack a strong adventitia and external elastic lamina, so they can present with subarachnoid hemorrhage. They are managed more like ruptured aneurysms: antithrombotics are avoided, and endovascular parent-vessel sacrifice or flow diversion may be used.
- Blunt cerebrovascular injury (BCVI) after trauma is screened with CTA using expanded Denver criteria. These include cervical fractures through the transverse foramen, C1-C3 fractures, Le Fort II/III patterns and skull-base fractures through the carotid canal. Biffl grading (I-V) guides antithrombotic versus endovascular management.
- Most dissections recanalize within months. Residual pseudoaneurysms rarely rupture and usually need no repair.

**Operative considerations in CEA.**
- Preoperative imaging should locate the bifurcation. A high bifurcation (at or above C2) may need subluxation of the mandible or division of the posterior belly of digastric. In that case transcarotid or transfemoral stenting may be preferable.
- Cerebral protection can be selective shunting, guided by awake neurological monitoring under regional anesthesia, EEG or stump pressure, or routine shunting. GALA found no outcome difference between general and local anesthesia.
- A non-recurrent right laryngeal nerve, associated with an aberrant right subclavian artery, can cross directly to the larynx at the operative level.
- **Cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome** (ipsilateral headache, seizures, hemorrhage) follows restoration of flow to a chronically dilated territory with impaired autoregulation. Strict postoperative blood pressure control matters.
- A neck hematoma after CEA can compromise the airway and is an emergency.

**Advances and open questions.** CREST showed similar composite outcomes for stenting and CEA. Stenting carried more periprocedural stroke, especially in older patients, while CEA carried more myocardial infarction. Transcarotid artery revascularization (TCAR) with flow reversal is expanding. With modern intensive medical therapy, the benefit of intervention for asymptomatic stenosis is being retested (CREST-2, ECST-2). Plaque imaging features such as intraplaque hemorrhage on MRI may better select patients than percent stenosis alone.

keyPoints: Dissection is blood within the arterial wall (intramural hematoma), causing stenosis or embolism
Spontaneous ICA dissection is usually distal cervical; vertebral dissection clusters at mobile V3 (C1-C2)
ICA dissection stretches the sympathetic plexus, giving painful partial Horner syndrome
Plaque forms at the carotid bulb, where wall shear stress is low and oscillatory
NASCET: CEA benefits symptomatic 70-99% stenosis most, ideally within about two weeks
CEA risks: hypoglossal, vagus/recurrent laryngeal, marginal mandibular nerves and the carotid sinus reflex

test.q: In an arterial dissection, blood collects:
test.explain: Dissection is an intramural hematoma: blood enters the wall, usually through an intimal tear.

test.q: Which sign is classic for internal carotid artery dissection?
choices: Loss of smell on one side
test.explain: The expanding wall stretches the sympathetic plexus on the ICA, giving ptosis and miosis with pain.

test.q: Why is facial sweating usually spared in carotid dissection Horner syndrome?
choices: Sweat fibers travel with the vagus nerve
Sweat fibers follow the external carotid
Sweat fibers exit at the jugular foramen
test.explain: Sudomotor fibers to the face run along the external carotid, so they are not stretched by an ICA hematoma.

test.q: Vertebral artery dissections most often occur in which segment?
test.explain: V3 is mobile around C1-C2, making it a common dissection site.

test.q: Which nerve crosses superficial to the ICA and ECA just above the bifurcation during CEA?
test.explain: CN XII crosses the carotids above the bifurcation. Injuring it weakens the tongue on that side.

test.q: Ligating which vein helps expose the carotid bifurcation?
test.explain: The common facial vein drains into the internal jugular vein at roughly the level of the bifurcation.

test.q: Manipulating the carotid sinus during surgery may cause:
test.explain: The baroreceptor reflex, carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve, slows the heart and lowers blood pressure.

test.q: Hoarseness after CEA most likely reflects injury to:
test.explain: The vagus nerve and its recurrent laryngeal branch control the vocal cords. Retraction can injure them.

test.q: Carotid plaque concentrates at the bulb mainly because of:
test.explain: Flow separation at the outer wall of the bulb creates low, oscillatory shear, which makes the endothelium pro-atherogenic.

test.q: The inner layer of the artery wall, where dissections usually start with a tear, is the ___.
test.explain: The intimal tear lets blood enter the media.

test.q: What is the surgery that removes plaque from inside the carotid artery called?
test.explain: The surgeon opens the artery and peels out the plaque.

test.q: The trial showing that CEA benefits symptomatic 70-99% stenosis is called ___.
test.explain: NASCET, published in 1991, established the benefit of CEA for symptomatic severe stenosis.

kidTest.q: Which arteries in the front of the neck carry blood to the brain?
kidTest.explain: The carotids run up the front of the neck.

kidTest.q: What happens in a dissection?
choices: Ice forms inside a frozen water pipe
Blood seeps between artery wall layers
A long bone snaps cleanly in half
kidTest.explain: A tear lets blood sneak into the wall of the artery.

kidTest.q: Where are the vertebral arteries found?
kidTest.explain: They travel through holes in the bones of the neck.

kidTest.q: What must surgeons protect when cleaning a carotid artery?
kidTest.explain: Small nerves lie right next to the carotid.

kidTest.q: Sticky gunk that clogs arteries is called p _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Plaque builds up and narrows arteries.

advancedTest.q: Fat-sat T1 MRI is normal 12 hours after a suspected ICA dissection. Best interpretation?
choices: Normal T1 signal points to vertebral rather than carotid disease
Early hematoma may not appear bright before methemoglobin forms
Intramural blood is brightest at once and fades over later days
Dissection is excluded because the wall looks normal
advancedTest.explain: The hematoma becomes bright on T1 once methemoglobin forms, so very early MRI can miss it.

advancedTest.q: Why are intracranial dissections prone to subarachnoid hemorrhage?
choices: They lack a strong adventitia and external elastic lamina
They carry much higher pressure than cervical arteries
They have no intima for the tear to begin in
Their media is thicker than in neck vessels
advancedTest.explain: With thin outer layers, blood within the wall can break through into the subarachnoid space.

advancedTest.q: A 30% stenosis by NASCET method would read differently using ECST because:
choices: ECST used the bulb diameter as the denominator
ECST measured the external carotid branch
ECST measured flow speed rather than diameter
advancedTest.explain: ECST compared the residual lumen with the estimated bulb diameter, giving higher percentages than NASCET's distal-ICA method.

advancedTest.q: After CEA, ipsilateral headache and seizure with high blood pressure suggest:
choices: Vagal injury producing vocal cord palsy
advancedTest.explain: A chronically dilated territory cannot autoregulate the restored flow, so hyperperfusion can cause headache, seizures or hemorrhage.

lessons.title: Cervical Lymph Node Levels, Neck Dissection & Nerves at Risk

levels.kid:
Your neck has tiny bean-shaped helpers called **lymph nodes**. Think of them as little security guard stations. When germs or bad cells travel through your body, the guards try to catch them.

There are hundreds of these guard stations in the neck. Doctors split them into groups, like rooms in a house, and give each room a number from 1 to 6. That way every doctor knows exactly which room they mean.

Sometimes a cancer from the mouth or throat sneaks into these nodes. Then a surgeon may carefully take out the nodes in the right rooms. That surgery is called a **neck dissection**.

The tricky part is that nerves run right next to the nodes, like wires behind a wall. Surgeons work slowly so they do not cut those important wires.
levels.hs:
The neck contains roughly 300 of the body's 800 or so **lymph nodes**. Lymph nodes are small filters along lymph vessels that trap germs and cancer cells. Cancers of the mouth, throat and voice box often spread to them first. The spread follows predictable paths, so surgeons divide the neck into numbered **levels**:

- **Level I**: under the chin (IA) and under the jaw (IB, around the submandibular gland)
- **Levels II, III, IV**: along the internal jugular vein, from top to bottom (upper, middle, lower jugular)
- **Level V**: the posterior triangle, behind the sternocleidomastoid muscle
- **Level VI**: the central neck, around the thyroid and trachea

A **neck dissection** is surgery to remove the nodes in chosen levels. A **radical neck dissection** removes levels I-V plus three structures: the **sternocleidomastoid muscle**, the **internal jugular vein** and the **spinal accessory nerve** (cranial nerve XI). Modern surgeons usually spare these when the cancer allows.

Nerves at risk include:
- **Spinal accessory nerve**: injury weakens the trapezius, causing shoulder droop and pain.
- **Marginal mandibular nerve**: a facial nerve branch; injury causes a lopsided lower lip.
- **Hypoglossal nerve**: injury weakens the tongue.

Example: a tongue cancer typically drains first to levels I-III. Surgeons therefore often remove just those levels in a **selective neck dissection**.
levels.college:
The level system (Memorial Sloan Kettering, later standardized by the American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, AAO-HNS) uses landmarks visible at surgery and on imaging.

- **IA** (submental): between the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles, above the hyoid. **IB** (submandibular): bounded by the digastric bellies and the mandible.
- **II** (upper jugular): skull base to the hyoid (clinically) or carotid bifurcation (surgically). The spinal accessory nerve splits it into **IIA** (in front of the nerve) and **IIB** (behind and above it).
- **III** (middle jugular): hyoid to the cricoid's lower border.
- **IV** (lower jugular): cricoid to the clavicle.
- **V** (posterior triangle): between the sternocleidomastoid's posterior border, the trapezius and the clavicle. The cricoid plane divides it into **VA** and **VB**.
- **VI** (central): hyoid to the suprasternal notch, between the carotids. Also called the anterior compartment.
- **VII**: the superior mediastinum, down to the innominate artery.

**Drainage predicts metastasis.** The oral cavity drains to I-III, the oropharynx, larynx and hypopharynx to II-IV, and the thyroid to VI. Nasopharyngeal cancer often reaches V and the retropharyngeal nodes.

**Types of dissection.**
- **Radical**: removes I-V plus the SCM, IJV and CN XI.
- **Modified radical**: removes I-V but spares one or more of those three structures.
- **Selective**: removes only the at-risk levels. Examples are supraomohyoid (I-III) and lateral (II-IV).
- **Extended**: removes extra nodes or structures beyond a radical dissection.

**Nerves at risk.**
- **CN XI**: in level IIB and across the posterior triangle. Injury causes **shoulder syndrome**: pain, drooping shoulder and poor abduction above 90 degrees.
- **Marginal mandibular branch of CN VII**: in level IB.
- **Hypoglossal (CN XII)**: deep in levels I-II.
- **Vagus (CN X)**: in the carotid sheath.
- **Phrenic nerve**: on the anterior scalene. Injury paralyzes half of the diaphragm.
- **Recurrent laryngeal nerve**: in level VI.
- **Sympathetic trunk**: injury causes Horner syndrome.
- **Thoracic duct**: at the left level IV root. Injury causes a chyle leak.
levels.phd:
**Historical arc.** George Crile described en bloc radical neck dissection in 1906. Hayes Martin popularized it at Memorial Sloan Kettering in the 1950s. Function-preserving surgery followed: Osvaldo Suárez and later Ettore Bocca developed fascial-compartment ('functional') dissection. The argument was that nodes sit inside fascial envelopes separable from the SCM, IJV and CN XI. Jatin Shah's 1990 analyses of node-positive mapping in previously untreated patients defined predictable level-specific spread. Oral cavity primaries rarely skip to IV or V; oropharyngeal and laryngeal primaries favor II-IV. Isolated level V disease without disease at other levels is uncommon. These data justified selective dissection. Robbins led AAO-HNS classifications (1991, 2002, 2008) that tied boundaries to radiologic landmarks, enabling CT/MRI staging. A 2011 Ferlito-Robbins proposal suggests naming dissections by the levels and structures removed, e.g., 'ND (I-III)'.

**Skip metastases.** In oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma, Byers reported direct metastasis to level IV in roughly 10-16% of cases. This drives debate over including level IV in elective dissection for tongue primaries.

**Level IIB nuance.** IIB is rarely involved in the absence of IIA disease. Yet dissecting IIB requires the most traction on CN XI, which correlates with postoperative shoulder dysfunction. Many surgeons omit IIB in clinically N0 oral cavity and laryngeal cancers.

**CN XI anatomy.** The nerve exits the jugular foramen and crosses the IJV, usually laterally (in about 70% of cases), though medial crossing and passage through a fenestrated IJV occur. It enters the SCM's deep surface. It then emerges near **Erb's point**, roughly 1 cm above the great auricular nerve's emergence along the posterior SCM border, and runs obliquely across the posterior triangle to the trapezius. Cervical plexus contributions (C2-C4) vary in their motor role, which partly explains variable deficit severity.

**Marginal mandibular nerve.** Dingman and Grabb's dissections found the nerve above the inferior mandibular border in about 81% of sides posterior to the facial artery. In the rest it dipped up to roughly 1 cm below. The **Hayes Martin maneuver** ligates the facial vein low and reflects it superiorly to protect the nerve.
levels.expert:
**Elective neck management in the N0 neck.** D'Cruz et al. (NEJM 2015) randomized patients with early oral cavity SCC to elective versus therapeutic dissection. Elective dissection improved 3-year overall survival (about 80% vs 68%). This settled a long controversy for primaries with relevant invasion depth. Depth of invasion now enters AJCC 8th edition T staging, and many teams use about 3-4 mm as a threshold for treating the neck. **Sentinel lymph node biopsy** is an alternative in early oral cancer. SENT and the Japanese JCOG1601 trial suggest it is non-inferior with less morbidity. Floor-of-mouth primaries are tricky because the injection site sits close to level I ('shine-through').

**HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer** often presents with cystic level II nodes, sometimes mistaken for branchial cleft cysts in adults. Any adult with a 'branchial cyst' deserves workup for an occult primary. AJCC 8 stages HPV-positive disease separately. **Extranodal extension** (ENE) is the key adverse nodal feature. Together with positive margins it indicates adjuvant chemoradiation (EORTC 22931/RTOG 9501 pooled data).

**Pitfalls.**
- **Chyle leak**: occurs in about 1-2.5% of dissections, mostly on the left at level IV. Recognize milky drain output that increases with enteral feeding. Prevent by a Valsalva check before closure.
- **Bilateral IJV sacrifice**: can cause facial edema, raised intracranial pressure and SIADH-like states. Stage the procedures or preserve one vein.
- **Carotid blowout**: risk rises with irradiated necks, fistulas and flap failure. Coverage with a pectoralis or other vascularized flap helps protect the vessel.
- **Shoulder syndrome**: can occur even with CN XI preserved, from devascularization or traction. Early physiotherapy is advised. Nerve monitoring (EMG) is increasingly used.
- **Post-radiation salvage**: fibrosis obliterates planes and raises complication rates. After chemoradiation, PET-CT surveillance (PET-NECK trial, 2016) safely avoids planned dissection in complete metabolic responders.

**Open questions.** Open questions include how far de-escalation can go in HPV-positive disease and whether to dissect level IIB and level IV routinely. Further questions are whether sentinel node biopsy can replace elective dissection broadly and whether robotic or retroauricular approaches reduce morbidity.

keyPoints: Neck nodes are mapped into levels I-VI (plus VII) by surgical and imaging landmarks
Primary site predicts drainage: oral cavity to I-III, larynx/pharynx to II-IV, thyroid to VI
Radical neck dissection removes levels I-V plus SCM, internal jugular vein and CN XI
Modified radical spares those structures; selective removes only at-risk levels
CN XI injury causes shoulder syndrome; marginal mandibular injury distorts the lower lip
Other risks: hypoglossal, vagus, phrenic, sympathetic trunk, and left-sided chyle leak

test.q: Which three structures are removed in a classic radical neck dissection, besides levels I-V?
choices: SCM, internal jugular vein, CN XI
Phrenic nerve, trapezius, external jugular vein
test.explain: A radical dissection removes the sternocleidomastoid, internal jugular vein and spinal accessory nerve. The carotid and vagus are preserved.

test.q: Level VI lymph nodes are located in the:
test.explain: Level VI is the central neck around the thyroid and trachea, from the hyoid to the suprasternal notch.

test.q: Which nerve divides level II into IIA and IIB?
test.explain: Level IIA lies in front of CN XI and IIB lies behind and above it.

test.q: After neck dissection, a patient has a drooping, painful shoulder and cannot lift the arm overhead. Which nerve was most likely injured?
test.explain: CN XI supplies the trapezius. Injury produces shoulder syndrome. Long thoracic injury causes scapular winging and is not a typical neck dissection injury.

test.q: Oral cavity cancers most commonly drain first to which levels?
test.explain: The oral cavity drains to levels I-III, which is why the supraomohyoid dissection removes these.

test.q: A dissection removing levels I-V but sparing the internal jugular vein is called:
test.explain: A modified radical dissection removes levels I-V but preserves one or more of the SCM, IJV and CN XI.

test.q: Injury to the marginal mandibular nerve causes:
choices: Loss of taste on the tongue
test.explain: This facial nerve branch moves lower-lip depressors. Tongue weakness would come from hypoglossal injury.

test.q: Milky drain fluid after a left level IV dissection suggests injury to the:
test.explain: The thoracic duct joins the venous system at the left root of the neck. Injury causes a chyle leak.

test.q: Level V corresponds to which region of the neck?
test.explain: Level V lies behind the SCM, in front of the trapezius and above the clavicle.

test.q: Surgery that removes only the node levels at highest risk is called a ___ neck dissection.
test.explain: Selective dissections, such as supraomohyoid (I-III), reduce morbidity.

test.q: Injury to which nerve, lying on the anterior scalene, paralyzes half of the diaphragm?
test.explain: The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) runs on the anterior scalene and supplies the diaphragm.

test.q: Which cranial nerve (by number) is the hypoglossal nerve?
test.explain: The hypoglossal nerve is CN XII. It runs deep in levels I-II and moves the tongue.

kidTest.q: What do lymph nodes in the neck do?
kidTest.explain: They act like guard stations that trap germs and bad cells.

kidTest.q: How do doctors label the groups of neck nodes?
kidTest.explain: Each group, like a room in a house, gets a number from 1 to 6.

kidTest.q: What is a neck dissection?
kidTest.explain: It is surgery that takes out nodes when a cancer has spread there.

kidTest.q: Why do surgeons work slowly in the neck?
kidTest.explain: Nerves run close to the nodes, like wires behind a wall.

kidTest.q: Lymph nodes are shaped like a little b _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Lymph nodes are small and bean-shaped.

advancedTest.q: Why do many surgeons omit level IIB in clinically N0 oral cavity cancer?
choices: IIB nodes drain mainly the thyroid and are handled in level VI
IIB lies inside the carotid sheath and is unsafe to reach
IIB is rarely involved without IIA, yet dissecting it strains CN XI
IIB is the main route for skip metastases to level IV
advancedTest.explain: Isolated IIB disease is uncommon, and IIB dissection requires traction on CN XI that correlates with shoulder dysfunction.

advancedTest.q: Byers' finding of direct level IV metastasis in some oral tongue cancers implies what about a standard I-III dissection?
choices: It should be replaced by radical dissection in most cases
It overtreats because tongue cancers spread to level VI
It may miss occult disease in some tongue primaries
It removes more nodes than the D'Cruz trial supported
advancedTest.explain: Skip metastases to IV (roughly 10-16%) fuel debate about extending dissection to level IV for tongue primaries.

advancedTest.q: A patient keeps an anatomically intact CN XI yet develops shoulder syndrome. The best explanation is:
choices: Traction or devascularization of the preserved nerve
Accidental removal of the levator scapulae muscle
Phrenic nerve injury weakening the trapezius
Marginal mandibular injury spreading to the shoulder
advancedTest.explain: Shoulder syndrome can occur despite preservation because of traction or devascularization. Variable C2-C4 contributions also affect severity.

advancedTest.q: Why is bilateral simultaneous internal jugular vein sacrifice avoided?
choices: It cuts off the arterial blood supply to the brainstem
It usually damages the thoracic duct on both sides
It denervates the trapezius on both sides of the neck
It blocks venous outflow, causing edema and high ICP
advancedTest.explain: Losing both IJVs obstructs cerebral and facial venous outflow, causing facial edema and raised ICP. Procedures are staged or one vein is preserved.
